title: Council Post: AI: Has The Student Become The Teacher?
text:
As marketing director of Attensi, Anthony Wong helps people learn faster and better by making learning more fun and fruitful.
ChatGPT has as many people scared as it does excited. Popular culture has many of us believe that the development of AI is akin to bringing dinosaurs back to life and that humanity’s desire for progress will eventually be its downfall.
The Terminator, 2001: A Space Odyssey and more recently Ex Machina, all depict an AI that goes rogue and turns on its human creators in a fantastically violent fashion. As is often the case, the reality is far less cinematic.
The World Economic Forum, WEF, has predicted that more work tasks will be handled by machines in a “robot revolution,” leaving many people out of work. This brings about the problem of millions of workers needing to be reskilled, and I want to question whether the root of this trouble also holds the solution.
The State Of Play
In the ever-changing landscape of business, the need for high-level digital skills is set to increase by 55%. Learning and development need to be at the forefront of every business to meet these growing needs.
One study shows that a company with a 10,000-plus strong workforce can spend over 100 hours training each employee. Ineffective training can cost up to $13.5 million per 1,000 employees per annum.
Simply put, it’s unsustainable and unprepared for the future. A serious revamp is needed. Industry leader Josh Bersin believes AI has a bigger part to play.
Could AI Be The Future Of L&D?
Bersin believes that the prospect of ChatGPT and AI presents “enormous opportunities.” He points to an AI that he has seen create educational content such as quizzes and course outlines, content which “typically takes a lot of cognitive effort.” ChatGPT has been used to do the same, creating a three-hour course complete with a test in just 10 hours.
AI, when applied like this, could save an untold amount of time and money when training and reskilling employees and completely change L&D as we know it. That is, if the content it generates is factual.
The Tortoise And The Hare
Slow and steady wins the race, right? The speed of ChatGPT is undeniable. It’s the proverbial hare in this story. But a course filled with misinformation is useless compared to a more traditional method, whether it’s made in 10 hours or 10 minutes.
How do we know if an AI-generated course is factual or not?
The truth is, we don’t.
Even on the ChatBot’s prompt page, there is a warning that it “may occasionally generate incorrect information.” Professor Michael Wooldridge, director of foundational AI research at the Alan Turing Institute in London, says ChatGPT “doesn’t know what’s true or false” and that fact-checking is necessary to use it.
“If you ask it for a recipe for an omelet, it’ll probably do a good job, but that doesn’t mean it knows what an omelet is.” ChatGPT, and AI in general, is very much a work in progress and probably not quite ready to step into the shoes of more traditional learning methods yet.
‘Don’t Believe Everything You See On The Internet’
We’ve all heard that famous phrase, right? ChatGPT was raised on the internet. Everything it “knows” is sourced from it. But, as discussed above, it doesn’t know the difference between true and false. Bersin believes this to be the reason for AI’s shortcomings.
Luckily, it presents an obstacle that he believes can be overcome fairly easily. What ChatGPT represents is software that can regurgitate and formulate information at incredible speeds, and so long as your source is legitimate, what it produces will be.
Bersin says “If you focus the AI on a trusted domain of content (most companies have oodles of this), it can solve the ‘expertise delivery’ problem at scale.” This type of AI would have “hundreds of applications in business” and revolutionize the way we train.
C-3PO Or Skynet?
It’s plain to see the humongous impact AI will have on not just the business world. But the mystery of whether the impact will be good or bad remains. Will it be a helpful source of information—a C-3PO to humanity’s Luke Skywalker—or will our creation turn on us?
Whichever it is, there’s no doubt that AI could become a huge feature of learning and development. Chatbots like ChatGPT are only going to become more sophisticated, and it’s already at a very impressive level.
AI can help L&D specialists to create engaging content. In the future, it could assist them in creating content in different languages. This would be welcomed by enterprise businesses where that require consistency across the globe. Furthermore, I can see AI assisting L&D specialists in creating engaging graphics and taking out the creative headache. As many know, when you combine graphics with written content, you can create a winning formula for engaging content.
If we embrace the new technology, L&D can reach a scale of efficiency the likes of which we have never seen before. There is still progress to be made, but I’m not sure if we’re quite ready to ditch the old ways just yet!

title: From Tea Breaks To Oil Changes, Robots In The Warehouse
text:
No tomatoes. It’s now a common term among UK supermarket shoppers (for February and March 2023 at least) and it’s down to various forces affecting the European supply chain for the salad bowl and sandwich favourite. As the BBC has noted, poor weather is having a major impact on the supply chain and the after-effects of Brexit could also be to blame.
What’s for sure is that the post-pandemic populous are now all a whole lot more likely to understand what a supply chain is. They will also have an appreciation for why some of our store shelves are empty from time-to-time and be far more appreciative of basics like toilet paper and basic tinned goods when they are available as normal.
What the supply chain of the future will run on is a more concerted application of Articificial Intelligence (AI) and the use of Machine Learning (ML) to drive operational decisions. If we accept this new part of logistical engineering to be true, then how will ML drive the new robot supply chain workers that we all need and what governing factors do we need to think about?
Navigating macro headwinds
“This is already proving to be another complex year for businesses, with digital so critical for those wishing to navigate the sustained uncertainty and macro headwinds. Businesses need to be more connected to their customers than ever and digital software application development initiatives, including those focused on machine learning, are enabling them to do this,” said Lori Steele, president & chief revenue officer at Salesforce EMEA.
Steele says she is seeing an increasing number of companies, across sectors ranging from automotive to financial services, deploy cloud platforms to help them understand customers and their behavior patterns. Car makers, for example, are using real-time analytics in the cloud to deliver personalized customer experiences that continually adapt to changes and nuances in user habits.
Similarly (also drawing from the Salesforce customer experience folder) financial services firms are using targeted automation and AI to unlock insights into their clients, enabling them to better anticipate their needs and drive satisfaction at a time when expectations for convenience, reliability and service are soaring.
“Efficiency is especially key,” enthused Steele. “In the current inflationary environment, we see companies focused on time to value, reducing costs and consolidating vendor relationships. The cloud makes this possible, powering a 360-view of the supply chain that allows CEOs to be far more agile and impactful when key business decisions need to be made and quickly.”
Avoiding ‘useless’ machine learning
According to Aaron Kalb in his role as chief strategy officer & co-founder at data management specialist Alation, if organizations can’t find the right data, they can’t use the true power of machine learning data, so that element needs to be covered off first and foremost.
But, he says, ‘bad data’ (i.e. untrusted data that stems from issues like inconsistent data standards, non-compliance and lack of effective data cataloguing and data governance – is even worse.
“This leads to ‘useless’ machine learning tools and even exposes businesses to risk,” said Kalb. “Pumping biased, out-of-date, or otherwise low-quality training data into machine learning algorithms means that you’ll get poor predictions, classifications and automated decisions – garbage in, garbage out.”
The Alation team assert that errors like this (above scenario) can have disastrous consequences for manufacturers, distributors, retailers and customers across the entirety of the supply chain.
“The way to succeed with machine learning initiatives is to first solve the data literacy, data curation and data intelligence challenges. This way, organizations can easily find, understand, and, most importantly, trust the data that machine learning models rely upon,” added Kalb.
The real-time digital warehouse
Within all of this discussion, there appears to be a strong gravitational pull towards real-time data. Indeed, as far as Richard Jones is concerned in his position as VP for Northern Europe region at Confluent, disruptive commerce (and the whole move to digital ML-enriched supply chains) is predicated on timeliness.
“It’s not just about having the right product, but the ability to deliver it into the market at the perfect moment to make waves,” stated Jones. “The importance of speed places strain upon the supply chain. Real-time capture and analysis of logistical data is now fundamental to any meaningful attempt at long-term strategy.”
The Confluent VP further suggests that data analysis should extend beyond individual metrics i.e. the act of combining them to better understand emerging trends is crucial here. This matters because AI and ML can be used to identify and anticipate certain behaviors or situations, and ultimately automate responses to pivotal moments in the supply cycle.
“This foresight and proactivity is only possible as, while it’s traditionally performed by batch learning, ML is increasingly able (in the right infrastructure) to take place in real-time,” said Jones. “Businesses can quickly create predictive models to apply to data streams, accelerating time to maturity, while safe in the knowledge that those models are perpetually learning on the fly. For example, in the situation of a customer looking to purchase a highly personalized item like a car, the manufacturer could tie all the different data sources together in the supply chain to give details of when the car will be ready and also let the customer know that if perhaps one of the personalised items was changed the car would be available earlier. These data sources could also help with back-end operations and logistics, ensuring that all parts are readily available at the same time to build the vehicle together.”
As a result of software automation and machine learning's ability to deliver an acute ‘down-to-the-second’ understanding of how an organization's systems are working, we can perhaps hope for a future where our supply chains work with increased fluidity, efficiency and resilience.
If all that happens effectively, then ‘no tomatoes’ will no longer be the bemoaning cry of supermarket shoppers in post-Brexit Britain - instead, it will only be the answer to that favorite children's joke: what’s red and invisible?

title: Council Post: Is AI-Powered Personalization A Game-Changer For Logo Designers?
text:
Zaheer Dodhia, CEO of Logo Design, is an entrepreneur who’s launched multiple startups, including ZillionDesigns, PCStore, CashforUsedLaptop
The world of logo design is constantly growing, fluctuating, pioneering—and sometimes, apparently, developing a mind of its own. Yes, artificial intelligence has been a factor in graphic design for some years now, but it’s getting down to a big question: Is AI the game-changer that designers have been looking for?
The chief player in the usefulness of AI in design could be pinned on the question of personalization. Any print-on-demand site offers AI-powered design generation that allows the user to input criteria and see them displayed on a variety of products. But logo design requires a higher level of personalization, simply because a business logo is the single piece of design that will carry the bulk of recognition and brand building. Logo design sites like mine that rely heavily on AI also need a more detailed algorithm in order to consistently provide worthwhile design.
When it comes to logo design, personalization can provide the hat trick that companies are looking for:
• Fits the brand personality.
• On-message.
• Memorable.
• Totally unique.
But is AI-powered personalization the tool that will alter the way logo designers operate for good?
AI-Driven Personalization In Brand Design
As a serial entrepreneur with a number of ventures under my belt, I appreciate any tool that streamlines the process of developing a new brand. While I highly value the designers I’ve worked with throughout my career, I also highly value anything that can keep my budget and timeline for launch as trim as possible.
This is not to say, of course, that human designers and AI design are mutually exclusive. Graphic designers that make good use of AI-powered personalization can potentially provide their logo design clients with a wider range of options in a shorter period of time. And in my experience, including AI as a tool rather than a whole-cloth solution is to the benefit of both entrepreneurs and graphic designers—but that’s a whole different article.
According to the recent paper "Design in the Age of Artificial Intelligence" published by Harvard Business School, "AI does not undermine the basic principles of design thinking," but it does "profoundly change the practice of design." From the creative brief to the delivery of the finished product, AI personalization can streamline the job of a logo designer.
Checking The Boxes
For the purposes of logo design, AI-powered personalization can be as simple as a "checking-the-boxes" scenario. The creative brief gives the designer the insight they need into the brand, which can then be input into the AI software to generate suggestions and solutions.
The chief aspect of this "checking-the-boxes" approach to design that may drastically change the game for logo designers? The fact that it makes design so much more accessible to everyone—not just experienced graphic designers. If it’s just a question of making sure your brand name is spelled right and that you choose a graphic you like, then sure, anyone can do it.
Of course, having dabbled in logo design myself and having worked with professional designers, I always recommend benefiting from the experience of others when you have the chance. That’s just good business sense. At the same time, I don’t think anyone has the right to gatekeep the tools of design. If AI will help an entrepreneur develop her logo without having to break her startup budget, it’s all worth it—even if it does change things somewhat for the logo designers who might otherwise have been working on that particular project.
But AI has other uses for professional logo designers.
Building A Catalog
One of the most time-consuming aspects of logo design is iteration. Designers will often produce a few potential concepts for their clients, giving them some choices. But once a design is decided upon for further development, the iteration process begins: tweaking this element, then that one, changing the colors, adjusting the fonts, circle versus square versus diamond and so on.
AI personalization is a boon for the iteration process, allowing designers to input their main parameters and then create an entire catalog of iterations, often within minutes or even seconds, just as a logo creator tool would do.
I can see this being a major game-changer, especially for independent logo designers, simply because it not only streamlines the process but actually cuts down on the time that iteration would otherwise take. This is better for the designer and better for the client—definitely a worthwhile tool for designers to incorporate.
Looking Ahead With AI
At times in the past, I’ve been somewhat on the fence about the use of AI in graphic design and other disciplines. Do we run the risk of missing out on what makes the design truly creative—the human touch?
But then I start to analyze the potential for benefits with AI tools, and I’m constantly reminded that it’s a question of forward movement.
One of the most important features of good AI-powered design software, in my experience, is the level of ability to differentiate and define more abstract concepts. You can tell AI software that you need a square logo with a squirrel for a mascot, with the company name incorporated. But it’s just as important to be able to define the tone, style and message of the logo (i.e., “fun,” “youthful” or “edgy”). This is still the prerogative of the human designer to a large degree; however, as machine learning continues to adapt, I expect the general tone-deafness of AI to gradually disappear, making AI design tools even more valuable for their users.
Is AI-powered personalization perfect? By no means. But does it have the potential to be a major game-changer for logo designers, both experienced and new? Absolutely.

title: Council Post: 14 Specialized Tech Leadership Roles That May Emerge In The Next Decade
text:
As technology continues to rapidly evolve, companies are starting to add new tech leadership roles to oversee the implementation and management of specific technologies and/or functions. Roles such as chief AI officer have emerged in recent years to help companies manage new and emerging tech platforms that didn’t exist even a decade ago.
In the next five to 10 years, tech experts expect to see even more tightly focused tech leadership roles added to companies’ headcounts. Below, a group of Forbes Technology Council members shares 14 specific roles they believe will emerge in the next decade and what those jobs will entail.
1. Quantum Computing Officer
As quantum computing technology continues to advance and become more practical for businesses, companies may begin to add a quantum computing officer role to their leadership teams to help navigate the complexities of this cutting-edge technology, as well as to identify and implement use cases where it can give them a competitive advantage. - Osama Sabbah, XPROfintech
2. CISO With Added OT Focus
Over the next five to 10 years, we’ll see the evolution of the role of industrial chief information security officer to become more business-oriented and include operational technology security. The CISO title focuses on “information,” but OT requires an understanding of business interruption, health and human safety, and the physics of an industrial process. Looking at the upcoming SEC and EU regulations, and it’s clear it’s inevitable—OT needs more attention. - Jason Christopher, Dragos
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. Data Ethics Officer
Within five to 10 years, I believe many conventional businesses will leverage artificial intelligence and big, sensitive data sets in a way that demands an executive focus on the ethical aspects of the application and use of these technologies. Data ethics officer, or perhaps AI ethics officer, could be an executive title that we will get used to hearing. - Jens Martin Skibsted, Manyone
4. Chief Data Officer
The journey toward more intelligent, data-driven outcomes means understanding and abstracting the value from data. Tech leaders need to have a solid understanding of not only AI systems, but also big data and its business implications. The chief data officer is an emerging tech leadership role that will be vital for companies looking to use data to inform their decisions and stay competitive. - Christine Boles, Intel
5. Chief Innovation Officer
With any new technology comes a spiked interest, and a common reaction from businesses is to create a specialized role in response. But with constant innovation, these roles can quickly become outdated once cutting-edge technology becomes a commodity. While chief innovation officer is not a new role, it is a requirement for companies wanting to make a dedicated shift toward emergent technologies. - Roman Reznikov, Intellias
6. Chief Compliance Officer
Privacy and data-management regulations continue to emerge across states and countries. Tracking and complying with these new laws is a full-time job, and the only way to truly master this challenge is through compliance automation. I expect the chief compliance officer to operate more like a CTO, with a much heavier emphasis on compliance management through automation. - Henri Isenberg, ReviewInc
7. Data Protection Officer
The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation calls for the mandatory appointment of a data protection officer at every organization. It’s anticipated that this call will stir things up amid the growing shift to a new era surrounding data privacy laws around the globe. With several states already planning to enforce GDPR statutes this year, online data privacy will become a driving role in organizational decision making in the near future. - Danny Allan, Veeam Software
8. Cybersecurity Officer
In the next five to 10 years, a highly specialized cybersecurity officer position may emerge. As the number of cyber threats rises and the possible repercussions of a security breach become more severe, companies could start to give cybersecurity top priority as a crucial component of their technology strategies. - Neelima Mangal, Nutcache
9. Chief Data, Digital And Technology Officer
In the next five to 10 years, we will see the rise of the chief data, digital and technology officer. The role of the CIO has evolved as the world has shifted to a digital-first enterprise strategy. As a result, top CIOs are now the ringleaders choreographing data and analytics, as well as global digital and technology operations. As these core competencies continue to grow, the CIO role will expand to include data, digital and technology oversight. - Ankor Rai, EXL Service
10. Chief Artificial Intelligence Officer
I think we’re going to see the emergence of a new type of tech leadership role: the chief artificial intelligence officer. Companies will start to add a CAIO as someone to bridge the gap between the business and the technical side. The CAIO will be responsible for making sure that AI is being used appropriately, without bias and consistently with the company’s values. - Leon Gordon, Pomerol Partners
11. Compliance Officer
Compliance officers will become more commonplace in the next five to 10 years. In terms of cybersecurity, we are already seeing compliance standards being required to receive government funding. Within private companies, compliance standards only need to be met when getting cybersecurity insurance. With billions of dollars being lost to cyberattacks every year, it is a matter of when, not if, compliance will become mandatory across the board. - Ben Finke, OnDefend
12. Information Manager
Information management is needed at every company, but it’s often placed on the shoulders of data engineers, chief data and analytics officers, and IT managers. The reality is that information management is a discipline; it requires a holistic understanding of an ecosystem and continuous active organization of databases. I think we’ll start to see companies bring in these professionals to oversee the maintenance of their data platforms. - Lewis Wynne-Jones, ThinkData Works
13. DeFi Officer
The decentralized finance officer role could emerge in the next five to 10 years, as DeFi is rapidly gaining traction. Apart from researching and implementing DeFi projects and protocols, managing digital assets, and ensuring compliance with regulations, they’d also be responsible for staying up to date on the latest developments in the DeFi space. - Andres Zunino, ZirconTech
14. Customer Advocate
A customer advocate will be a highly professional and senior technology staff member who will attend all client meetings and listen to their needs. There is so much focus on the technologies, but really, we must focus on the customers’ needs. Technologies are a means to get to the end, which is meeting customer needs. - Maria Scott, TAINA Technology

title: Council Post: Generative AI: Education In The Age Of Innovation
text:
Geoffrey Alphonso, CEO at Alef Education.
The intelligence contained within artificial intelligence (AI) has been making significant leaps and bounds very recently, with generative AI becoming one of the most popular topics in the tech industry. Generative AI like ChatGPT has the potential to transform various industries, including education, potentially bringing the sector forward into an increasingly more technologically-heavy future for all the good and the bad that it brings.
Use Cases And Benefits Of Generative AI In Education
The potential applications of generative AI in the education sector are endless, with personalized learning content being one of many possibilities floating around the market. Experts believe that creating new and exciting products that utilize generative AI will better allow educators to create engaging and interactive learning experiences to help foster growth in their students.
Examples of generative AI use cases in education include:
• Generating questions for students to answer based on their current level of understanding and achievement.
• Generating personalized study plans for students based on their performance and strengths/weaknesses.
• Creating engaging and interactive learning activities, such as games and simulations, to help students understand complex concepts.
• Generating real-time feedback and assessments, allowing teachers to quickly identify areas where students need additional support.
Generative AI essentially produces content (e.g., text, images, audio, video) for the digital publishing industry in education, which can have huge cost reduction benefits. Furthermore, for personalized learning, generative AI potentially enables the provision of step-by-step problem-solving hints and feedback to learners. If designed well to encourage learner skill development, this could really help address teacher-related challenges, as AI can replace teacher tasks to provide individualized, real-time feedback. This is real, personalized learning.
Challenges And Limitations Of Generative AI In Education
While generative AI in education has numerous benefits, we must also remain aware and vigilant for potential drawbacks. One concern is the potential for bias in generated educational content, as the algorithms are only as unbiased as the data they are trained on. It is not impossible for a generative AI program that was created to be utilized by a particular group of students based on their race, gender or socioeconomic status could reinforce negative stereotypes and negatively impact their learning experience. Above all else, we must ensure generative AI systems are designed and programmed to be inclusive and equitable for all users.
Additionally, while generative AI systems may have seemingly endless applications in education, they may lack the creativity and originality human teachers and educators can provide. While humans can have boundless creativity and ingenuity, generative AI systems are limited by the data they have been provided, meaning they may lack the ability to produce content that is innovative or outside the box. So while generative AI may be the next big thing in education, we must remember that educators continue to play an invaluable and irreplaceable role in the learning process.
The potential for students to use and perhaps even rely too heavily on the technology to provide immediate answers and solutions will most certainly come up when addressing the use of AI in education, with many people fearing students will use generative AI to cheat. However, the real question is how to leverage generative AI to benefit learner skill development from now to the next 10 years. When introducing AI products into the classroom, care must be taken to ensure the technology does not hinder students' development of critical thinking and problem-solving skills or undermine the integrity of student work.
The digital divide between students with and without access to technology may also be exacerbated by the use of generative AI in education, potentially widening the learning gap for underserved and minority students. A good product that properly utilizes generative AI's capacity to benefit education requires "capacity" and visionary leadership support. "Capacity" means a team of educated domain experts who understand the potential of generative AI, data scientists and engineers who know how to work with domain experts to explore that potential and iterate on solutions. Leadership is extremely essential to connect these experts and provide the necessary resources and support to make this happen.
Future Implications Of Generative AI In Education
Education is rapidly evolving, and generative AI is likely to play a major role in shaping its future. We can anticipate seeing cutting-edge generative AI applications in education as the technology develops. For instance, generative AI could be used to create virtual teachers that would provide students with 24/7 support, allowing them to learn at their own pace and on their own schedule. This could be particularly beneficial for students in remote or underserved areas who may not have access to traditional classroom-based education.
Generative AI could also be used to create adaptive learning experiences that would adjust in real time to students' needs and abilities. This could be done by using generative AI systems to analyze students' learning patterns and preferences and then adapting the content and teaching methods accordingly. This would allow students to receive more targeted and effective support and achieve better learning outcomes.
When it comes to best practices for using generative AI in education, there is not much established yet, as this is a new domain with many possibilities. However, as industry leaders, to address potential ethical and privacy concerns and to develop solutions that benefit human development for the upcoming decade, it is important to build the "capacity" and vision to connect cross-disciplinary experts to explore, iterate and test with pilot users before launching in education systems. This is the only way to embrace technology and build solutions that benefit learners and teachers. I believe the industry has the advantage and ability to do so.
Conclusion
On the whole, generative AI has the potential to complement educators and the EdTech sector in a multitude of creative and time-saving ways, revolutionizing the traditional classroom setting. However, there is no reward without risk, and education stakeholders must remain vigilant of potential drawbacks and challenges related to bringing generative AI solutions into schools.

title: Council Post: Prepare For The AI Phishing Onslaught
text:
As Chief Executive Officer at IRONSCALES, Eyal Benishti pioneered a leading self-learning anti-phishing email security solution.
By now, you’ve probably heard of Open AI’s ChatGPT, a free AI-driven chatbot that generates well-written, convincing content in English and other languages and can even write and debug software code. It has been called an AI tipping point, and its implications for everything from college student essays to marketing content and software development are startling, to say the least.
There’s another area for which ChatGPT and its AI competitors have startling implications as well: phishing. I’m not just talking about an AI-empowered leap in phishing sophistication but phishing volume as well. In fact, the implications are so devastating and potentially overwhelming for IT organizations that the only way to fight back against this AI weapon is with other AI weapons.
Better, Bigger And Riskier
Why do ChatGPT and similar tools have huge implications for the battle against phishing?
Perfect English
Gone are the telltale English spelling and grammar errors that alerted humans and tools to phishing emails until now. As with college essays and marketing content, ChatGPT can generate beautifully written, well-structured emails on just about any subject. Enter, “Write an email from the company CEO to employees, subject Urgent Action Required, New Stock Options Plan Announced. Urge employees to click on the attachment today,” and in seconds, ChatGPT will generate a beautifully written, grammatically flawless email doing just that. Foreign hackers can even write phishing emails in another language and use ChatGPT to translate them into perfect English, not to mention enhance them.
Continuous Refinement
Hackers can use ChatGPT to refine phishing emails again and again, regenerating them in different and better permutations and styles. They can ask ChatGPT to suggest ideas to convince recipients to open an attachment today. They can train AI tools on large datasets of previous phishing emails or emails from legitimate company senders to generate more convincing phishing emails and create new types of attacks that evade phishing detection systems. Users can leverage scripts that search LinkedIn and other social media for target company executive and staff names and titles and feed the information to ChatGPT to generate personalized phishing emails.
Phishing Volume
Get ready for a flood of phishing emails now that hackers don’t have to spend time writing and refining them themselves. Expect the flood to overwhelm users, traditional email filtering tools and security and IT departments. Prepare for an exponential increase in the number of hackers since nobody needs hacking sophistication to phish anymore, and for the use of automated tools on the dark web that empower anyone to generate thousands of automated personalized phishing emails for multipronged phishing attacks.
Even the best-trained employees will find it increasingly difficult to cope with the huge volumes of higher-quality phishing emails to come. IT departments will likely be overwhelmed by the number of user-reported phishing emails and unreported emails that bypass traditional defenses.
Coding
Aside from text, ChatGPT can generate very usable code for convincing web landing pages, invoices for business email compromise (BEC) attempts and anything else hackers need it to generate.
AI Is The Problem, And AI Is The Solution
How can companies combat the overwhelming volume of AI-empowered phishing attacks? Certainly not with legacy tools and user training alone. The answer to AI-empowered phishing lies in AI anti-phishing weaponry.
AI-empowered tools have the scale and smarts to address the higher phishing volumes to come. They can harness their understanding of email content, context, metadata and trusted behavior to detect anomalies characteristic of phishing attempts across hundreds of thousands of emails.
By training themselves on legitimate email content and context, AI tools can determine instantly if an email’s language content and style resemble that of equivalent past emails from legitimate senders. They can evaluate whether an email has come at roughly the same time and day of the month from the same sender as past similar emails, whether it uses the same path to traverse the Internet and contains the same email headers, bank account numbers and customer IDs. Zero trust is essential in a phishing environment with such high volumes.
Don’t Forget Training
It may be tempting to give up on user training with this powerful new threat, but doing so would be a big mistake. As I noted in a previous article, AI may be a critical weapon in the battle against phishing, but users will always be the last line of defense, even at the phishing volumes and sophistication we can expect in the years ahead.
As always, educate users continually on the latest phishing strategies, including AI-generated phishing emails. Take advantage of ChatGPT and similar tools to test users with their perfectly generated emails. Communicate the message constantly that we’re all living in a new world where anyone can create convincing phishing emails. Train them to always ask themselves the following: Does this email make sense compared to previous equivalent emails? Is it the right sender, the right time of day, week, month, etc.? Teach them to verify potential phishing emails through other channels as necessary. Give them the means to report suspicious emails quickly and easily and then feed that knowledge into your anti-phishing tools right away.
This is just the dawn of the age of the AI-generated hack. Expect more leaps in both AI-empowered hacking strategies and anti-hacking weaponry. Every organization must ensure it is ready for this new AI world. We knew this was coming, but it turned out to be even sooner and faster than we imagined. Look out for AI tools from Baidu, Google, Deep Mind, Character AI and others in the months to come.

title: Will ChatGPT Replace Your Job?
text:
ChatGPT has been all the rage. So what is it?
ChatGPT is an AI chatbot that’s a human-like conversationalist. The dialogue format and training make it possible for ChatGPT to answer follow-up questions, admit mistakes, challenge incorrect premises, and reject inappropriate requests. ChatGPT is OpenAI’s sibling to their InstructGPT model, which was trained to follow instructions and provide a detailed response.
The premise is that OpenAI trains, rather than programs, their AI models imply a more human-like quality to these artificially intelligent software applications. There’s no doubt that some components of human-held jobs will be replaced as AI continues to advance. But just as some become obsolete, others will thrive, and others will work side-by-side with AI.
Here are three jobs some researchers believe will be replaced by AI and how you can pivot your role to take advantage of this technology to advance your career:
1. Content Writer
ChatGPT can write grammatically correct, readable articles solely based on its training data. It cannot generate original content or make editorial decisions. ChatGPT lacks empathy and originality. It’s also recognized as AI-generated content most of the time by plagiarism and AI detectors like Originality.AI. That won’t necessarily hurt SEO ranking, as some SEO experts assert. Google is against spammy automatically generated content — regardless of whether a robot or a human writes it.
All of this points to good news for content writers. Use ChatGPT to write evergreen articles and generate keywords and quality backlinks. Let ChatGPT do the heavy lifting and the time-consuming work. Once that’s done, writers can humanize the content and make it shine. Writers add flare, creativity, and originality. Good writing is in the details, which require a human touch.
2. Computer Programmers and Coders
ChatGPT and other AI tools can write code more quickly and accurately than human programmers, provided these AI tools receive prompts. Most of the code written by AI is simple and serves a particular function. AI can’t analyze problems with the code or come up with solutions. AI doesn’t have the critical thinking skills to work through complicated programming.
Coders and programmers also fix bugs and improve existing code, so programs run more efficiently. AI is not capable of adequately forecasting human needs. However, the two — humans and bots — will likely work side-by-side in this field, where AI takes over the mundane and repetitive tasks, and humans focus on the creative and analytical side.
3. Financial Analysts, Advisors, and Bankers
AI can analyze and manipulate data sets faster and more efficiently than humans. Using AI allows financial advisors to forecast better investment mixes for their clients … so long as humans can interpret the data. AI is already used for investing. Robo Advisors use algorithms or AI to make changes to investment portfolios, and chatbots are used to provide financial advice.
But there will always be a need for human expertise and judgment. Only people can give personalized advice to their clients based on their unique circumstances. People in finance should focus on relationships and cultivating trust with their clients.
Another consideration is the tightly regulated financial industry. Laws will likely be passed to regulate how AI is used within this industry. Currently, AI has little oversight or accountability. It is a “big black box.” So, while AI has many benefits, it won’t replace financial jobs soon. Nonetheless, about 32% of banks currently use AI technology for repetitive tasks, fraud protection, personalized services, and other services. AI technology is projected to save North American banks as much as $70 billion by 2025.
AI is very good at doing what it is programmed to do, and you may compete with ChatGPT for an entry-level job. Still, it is unlikely to fully replace the seasoned programmer, writer, or [insert job title here].
AI will infiltrate every industry on some level. ChatGPT is just a few months old and already shaking up the workforce in many industries. The question is how entry-level applicants will compete against this evolving technology. People will need to focus on what AI cannot do: creative and artistic work or work requiring thoughtful analysis. In essence, be human.

title: Council Post: Consider The Risks Of Generative AI Before Adopting Game-Changing Tools
text:
Principal Research Director, Info-Tech Research Group. Author of Info-Tech's 2023 Tech Trends report.
When Prometheus stole fire from the gods to gift it to mortals, he enabled humans to begin civilization. But he still had to pay dearly for his crime, being bound to a rock as an eagle pecked out his liver.
The lesson of the Greek myth is that while new technology can bring revolutionary benefits, there is always a price to pay in exchange. Creators of new technology may be the focus of the ire, but its users can still get burned. It’s a myth that technology leaders should keep in mind as they consider the booming generative AI products market.
Last year saw image-generating bots emerge onto the scene, winning art contests and rapidly adopting users who enthusiastically shared their creations on social media. OpenAI’s ChatGPT emerged as the most compelling example of a large language model chatbot, now with 13 million daily users and the fastest-growing consumer application in history.
Generative AI tools are easily accessed from a web browser and can help workers shave hours off their daily tasks. From mocking up a design for a new website to writing employee communications or assisting in code development, the tools are flexible enough to help with any task. Organizations will consider adopting these new tools for their promise of productivity, but risks abound. Let’s consider the different types of risk ahead.
Legal: Copyright Questions Blur The Picture
Creators of generative AI products are the target of class-action lawsuits from plaintiffs that say their copyright has been infringed. At the heart of the issue is how the large models are trained. One case against Stability AI and Midjourney is from artists who say they never gave consent for their work to train AI. Now those companies are using their models to create derivative works that threaten the value of the original work from the actual artists.
Getty Images is also suing Stability AI, reports The Verge. Getty alleges that its database was scraped without its permission, and the images were used to train the model used by the firm’s image-generating bot, Stable Diffusion. Getty says it doesn’t consider this use to be covered by fair dealing in the U.K., where the lawsuit was filed, nor does it meet the bar for fair use in the U.S.
Legal experts say it’s difficult to consider what precedent a judge would use in making a decision on the matter. While attempts to protect an artist’s style with copyright haven’t been held up in the past, the models may be doing more than imitating the style of the images it was trained with. A group of researchers that extracted more than a thousand images from the models found that AI regurgitated exact copies of photographs of people, film stills and copyrighted press photos.
To understand how AI creators will defend themselves in court, look to the past publications of the lawyer hired by Stability AI—Mark Lemley, a professor of law at Stanford. In Fair Learning, he argues that AI should be able to use databases for training whether or not the contents are copyrighted. He claims that training sets contain millions of different works with different owners, so there is no plausible option to license all the content for new use. Therefore, allowing a copyright claim wouldn’t serve to benefit the copyright owners but only to deny the benefits of the new tool.
Image-generating AI isn’t the only type of AI feeling the heat. Github’s Copilot assists coders as they work, but a lawsuit alleges that it violates the open-source licenses of the code repositories that trained it. Microsoft, the owner of Github, says no harm is caused by Copilot and that it helps developers.
Businesses considering adopting generative AI tools may want to watch and see how a judge rules on these class-action lawsuits. In a scenario where the works generated by the tools are considered a copyright violation, organizations that publish them may also be considered at fault.
Reputation: Rage Against The Machine
As AI-generated content quickly moves from novelty to commonplace, people may grow tired of seeing it blasted all over the internet. Worse yet, as artists raise their voices to fight for their rights, many people will join their sides and react negatively to the use of AI-generated content.
When Netflix Japan tweeted a trailer for the upcoming short film The Dog & The Boy, admitting to using AI generative software to create background images because of a labor shortage, it got a lot of blowback. One artist alleged that Netflix expected creative work for free, while an AI engineer challenged the idea that there really was a labor shortage, offering to make connections to artists looking for work.
Many artist or developer communities are creating policies to ban AI-generated content rather than face backlash from their members.
Accuracy: Bias And Error
While the speed at which ChatGPT can provide comprehensive answers is incredible, those answers might not always hold up to scrutiny. Large models trained on data from the internet and other sources are prone to biases that could affect their output. They may also provide authoritative-sounding answers that are totally wrong.
OpenAI cofounder, Sam Altman, is aware of the tools’ weaknesses to the point that he described it as “incredibly limited…but good enough at some things to create a leading impression of greatness.” Altman recommends not using ChatGPT for important tasks.
Conclusion
Organizations that see generative AI as an exciting opportunity to augment their employees’ productivity should explore the tools. But they also need to consider what governance process is necessary to put in place now before the fire of generative AI burns out of control and opportunity turns into agony.

title: Council Post: Preparing For Business Success With Generative AI
text:
Chief Product Officer, CCC Intelligent Solutions Inc.
A few years ago, Andrew Ng predicted that AI would be the new electricity. Today while we are still absorbing all the many different ways AI can be applied, generative AI technologies like ChatGPT have taken the world by storm. Overnight the tone of the technology industry changed—going from gloom and doom to positive optimism about the huge opportunity around these new technologies. This area continues to attract huge investment—Microsoft pledged 10 billion of investment to OpenAI, and startups in this space have collectively raised over $1.5 billion in funding. The magnitude of impact is far-reaching—Google was reported to have declared “code red” internally due to the fear of this technology impacting search revenue. A race is on—in the same week, Google announced Bard, their conversational AI service, which will be released for beta testing, and Microsoft announced an updated Bing leveraging these technologies.
Generative AI technologies enable a whole host of potential use cases and applications. These use cases span a wide array, including creating content (e.g., Jasper.ai), creating presentations (e.g., Tome), writing code (e.g., MSFT Copilot or Replit), virtual assistants for writing essays or other content and virtual assistants for shopping or interviews, assistance in creating legal contracts, customer support, helping educators create personalized course content and so much more.
I had written about AI’s impact on the future of work earlier, including a 2x2 matrix showing the role of AI in enterprise applications based on the skill level of the user and the complexity of tasks performed. The fundamental parameters of the 2x2 are still relevant with generative AI, and one can superpose “creation” as a component of each quadrant (Analyze/recommend/create; Automate/ create; Assist/create; and Amplify/create.)
Based on the readiness of the technology and current limitations, today, the technology appears more suited for B2C scenarios that are not mission-critical (and, as a result, more forgiving). EY predicts knowledge management to be the killer use case for B2B scenarios. And while the technology may not yet be robust enough, make no mistake, with all the progress we have seen in the past few years, and the amount of investment going into this field, the technology will be ready for enterprise mission-critical applications before we know it. According to Satya Nadella, “the scale of the largest AI computation is doubling every six months, far outpacing Moore’s law.” There are a number of B2B use cases chomping at the bits to leverage these technologies.
Business leaders need to start thinking about how to prepare for these technologies—including how the business will make money (the monetization models) and what the organization needs to do to prepare for the future.
These technologies can open up new revenue streams for businesses. At the same time, applications will have to factor in the cost of using the technology, which today is still quite high. OpenAI, for example, has been contemplating a $20/user/month for the use of ChatGPT. Depending on how it is used, this can quickly ramp up and become quite expensive. For most companies having a clear monetization model is critical. Some of the models that can be contemplated for use include:
Subscription model: charging a monthly or per-user fee based on usage of the service, e.g., for customer support or virtual assistant. Companies can also consider starting with freemium services and then adding tiered pricing based on usage levels.
Pay-per-use model: charging based on the amount of usage of the service such as in content creation scenarios.
Platform model: charging for the use of the platform and enabling different tiers based on levels of usage.
Commission model: charging a percentage of transaction fees where the technology is being used to promote either sales (e.g., when using a virtual shopping assistant) or partner products (e.g., legal services).
Ad revenue model: similar to the above, but charging for promoting different services or offerings.
Value-based pricing: pricing based on value creation/effort reduction as a result of the use of the technology.
Premium model: embedding the technology into other product offerings and charging a premium for the use of the service.
Organizational readiness and change management are going to be an integral part of adopting these technologies. In order to prepare for this, leaders should start thinking about the following aspects.
• What are the areas of the business where this technology can be applied? A good way to start these discussions could be by engaging teams in hackathons, idea jams, etc., to collect different ideas.
• How can these technologies be integrated into existing systems and technology infrastructures to create the right value?
• Talent—what jobs will be done by people, and what jobs will be done by the AI? As a result, what skills will employees need, and how can they be upskilled/ trained?
• What is the impact on organizational structures? How do the current hierarchies and functional/ matrixed structures change?
• What are the organizational change management and communication plans to be put into place? How does one ensure there is clear communication and planning so employees understand the impact, the benefits and how technology will impact roles?
• How to set clear performance management objectives includes clarity on key metrics to understand whether these initiatives are delivering the desired outcomes.
• Addressing several key considerations around the use of the technology itself—including ethical considerations such as bias, explainability, model degradation, data privacy and security, trust and copyright/trademark issues.
• Understanding how to manage risk, including fraud, rethinking SLAs and legal agreements. For example, if there are errors, is the company delivering the solution responsible or the creator of the foundation models?
There is a lot of work to be done to get these technologies embedded into our natural ways of working—and make it as seamless as electricity. The path ahead for us is simultaneously exciting and mind-boggling!
